title: JMM targeted evidence source catalog
purpose: Searchable navigation and provenance; neither bibliography size nor appearance establishes eligibility.
limitations: Primary, synthesis, consensus, regulatory, expert-practice and candidate/unextracted sources coexist; read each context.
No source or protocol is automatically activated by this catalog.
Legacy repository sources are separately inventoried.

contexts.review_text: - **Sprint coaching, not an RCT:** Haugen et al. 2019 integrates research and elite practice and explicitly notes that much experimental sprint evidence comes from team sports. It describes acceleration work over 10–50 m with full recovery, and flying maximal-speed work over 10–30 m after individualized run-ins. Beginner/development examples use 20-m accelerations with ~2-min rest or 10-m flying sections with ~4-min rest; elite examples require much longer recovery. End on technical deterioration or performance drop-off. These are expert-practice ranges, not validated universal doses. [Full text; DOI 10.1186/s40798-019-0221-0](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-019-0221-0).

sources.verification_scope: See exact surrounding review context; full methods and numeric applicability are not assumed.

contexts.review_text: - **Elite threshold practice is descriptive:** Haugen and colleagues' 2024 Norwegian training-session study describes elite coaching, including double-threshold practice and approximate 2–4.5 mmol/L lactate targets. Coaches' successful practice does not isolate causality, establish novice safety, or mean every athlete's threshold is at that lactate. [Source; DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02067-4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-024-02067-4).

contexts.review_text: - **Concurrent training:** Schumann et al. 2022 meta-analysis of 43 studies found no clear average impairment of maximal strength or whole-muscle hypertrophy, but explosive strength gains could be attenuated, especially in the same session. Separation of at least 3 h was a subgroup distinction, not a proven exact recovery threshold. [PubMed; DOI 10.1007/s40279-021-01587-7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34757594/).

sources.verification_scope: See exact surrounding review context; full methods and numeric applicability are not assumed.

contexts.review_text: - **Taper:** Bosquet et al. 2007 pooled 27 studies; about 2 weeks and 41–60% volume reduction with intensity/frequency maintained was a useful competitive-athlete pattern, not a universal optimum. “Maintain intensity” means retaining some quality at reduced volume, not preserving the entire hard workload. [PubMed; DOI 10.1249/mss.0b013e31806010e0](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17762369/).

sources.verification_scope: See exact surrounding review context; full methods and numeric applicability are not assumed.

contexts.review_text: - **Load and safety:** IOC 2016 emphasizes individual, flexible external/internal load management including life stress, symptoms and recovery. Its historical numerical ACWR/10% examples should not be encoded as validated safety guarantees. [Consensus; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2016-096581](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096581). Impellizzeri et al. 2020 explains why causal injury-prevention claims from ACWR are unsupported. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32502973/).

contexts.review_text: - **Energy availability:** IOC 2023 REDs consensus applies across sexes; problematic under-fueling can compromise health and performance. A chatbot should not diagnose REDs from a score or prescribe aggressive weight loss to improve performance. Concerning symptoms warrant qualified assessment and stopping automatic load escalation. [Consensus; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994](https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/57/17/1073.long).

contexts.review_text: - `HYPR_VOLUME_OPTIMUM`: Replace “10–20 sets maximizes hypertrophy” with “Higher weekly set volume can produce larger average hypertrophy gains, with diminishing returns and individual variation; no universally optimal 10–20-set interval is established.” Schoenfeld et al. 2017 analyzed 15 studies using categories <5, 5–9 and 10+ sets, not a direct validation of a 10–20 optimum. [PubMed; DOI 10.1080/02640414.2016.1210197](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27433992/). Pelland et al. 2026 (online Dec 2025) included 67 studies/2,058 participants (79.1% male); models distinguish direct/indirect sets and show diminishing returns. This is meta-regression, not proof of an individual optimal dose. Supporting strength for endurance must not inherit a bodybuilding volume quota. [PubMed; DOI 10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41343037/).

contexts.review_text: Silva et al. 2010 randomized 239 women in a one-year weight-management program to an autonomy-supportive intervention versus general health education. Physical activity and autonomous motivation improved. This supports offering choice, meaningful goals and competence-building; it does not validate a particular chatbot phrase, compulsory athlete training dose, or coercive “push.” [Primary study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20012179/).

contexts.review_text: Nuss et al. 2023 tested motivational interviewing, a wearable tracker, both, or education in 40 insufficiently active adults over 12 weeks. contexts.review_text: | Daily carbohydrate | Conventional planning ranges: light/skill days 3–5 g/kg/day; moderate ~1 h/day 5–7; endurance ~1–3 h/day 6–10; very high load ~4–5 h/day 8–12. These are planning ranges, not mandatory ceilings or calorie prescriptions. | A for sufficient carbohydrate supporting glycogen-demanding training; actual need follows work and energy balance. | Requires actual body mass and actual load. Do not infer body mass from sex, sport or a sample athlete. Include exercise carbs in the daily total. [Thomas et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852). |

contexts.review_text: | Before competition / demanding prolonged exercise | 1–4 g/kg carbohydrate 1–4 h before, adapted to time available and tolerance. Carbohydrate loading for events >90 min: 10–12 g/kg/day for 36–48 h with reduced training, if appropriate. | A: glycogen availability; loading is relevant to prolonged competition, not every sprint or gym visit. | Smaller/less fibrous, lower-fat choices close to start can be easier to tolerate. Do not force maximum intake. No requirement for a glycogen-depletion phase. [Burke et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2011.585473). |

| During >2.5–3 h demanding exercise | Up to ~90 g/h using multiple-transportable carbohydrate is well-established; build and rehearse tolerance. | A for appropriate prolonged events. | Absolute g/h rather than automatic g/kg/h. These duration bins overlap intentionally; avoid a discontinuity at minute 75 or 150. [Burke carbohydrate guidance](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2011.585473), [Thomas position statement](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26891166/). |

- Avoid low-carbohydrate/fasted “train-low” blocks as a default performance enhancement. Adaptive signaling is not the same as improved competition performance; insufficient energy/carbohydrate and inability to complete the intended workload are meaningful downsides. [IOC carbohydrate review](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2011.585473), [IOC REDs 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994).

contexts.review_text: **Transport mechanism and gut practice.** Glucose and glucose polymers principally use SGLT1; fructose uses GLUT5. Combining transport pathways can raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation beyond single-source feeding. “60 g/h glucose ceiling” and “90 g/h total ceiling” are useful historical approximations, not universal hard biological limits. More absorption/oxidation does not automatically equal more race performance. A glucose:fructose ratio of 2:1 is established; newer high-intake studies use ~1:0.8 or 1:1. Do not describe any one ratio as optimal for everyone. [Currell & Jeukendrup 2008](https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0b013e31815adf19).

contexts.section: Sex, athlete level, low energy availability and anti-doping
contexts.review_text: **Sex and training level:** Many intervention studies are small and male-dominated; elite responses are not interchangeable with recreational responses. Female-inclusive swim studies help but do not solve gaps in long-event high-dose fueling, pregnancy, menopause, hormonal contraception or supplement interactions. Record population applicability. The [ISSN female-athlete statement 2023](https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2023.2204066) emphasizes energy adequacy and individual physiology; it is not authority to invent sex-only carbohydrate or sodium percentages. Menstrual symptoms, blood loss and health history can inform assessment when voluntarily provided. Do not diagnose hormonal state from calendar dates.

contexts.section: Sex, athlete level, low energy availability and anti-doping
contexts.review_text: **Low energy availability:** Persistent under-fueling can compromise health and performance in athletes of any sex/body size. Recurrent bone stress injury, menstrual disruption, reduced libido, persistent fatigue/illness, restrictive eating or unexplained performance decline warrant qualified evaluation. These are nonspecific signals, not an app diagnosis. Do not apply a universal 30 or 45 kcal/kg fat-free-mass threshold diagnostically, infer energy availability from BMI, or recommend intentional carbohydrate restriction when warning signs exist. [IOC REDs 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994). Avoid “earn your food” logic and do not subtract exercise carbohydrates from recovery meals automatically.

- Avoid low-carbohydrate/fasted “train-low” blocks as a default performance enhancement. Adaptive signaling is not the same as improved competition performance; insufficient energy/carbohydrate and inability to complete the intended workload are meaningful downsides. [IOC carbohydrate review](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2011.585473), [IOC REDs 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994).
